notes: Quantitative spine for the privacy study: how fast data privacy law spread (Greenleaf's global count, UNCTAD, US states), what notice-and-consent costs people (McDonald & Cranor; Obar & Oeldorf-Hirsch; Amos et al.; Pew 2019/2023), how consent pop-ups actually behave after the GDPR (Degeling et al.; Nouwens et al.), the scale of tracking and data brokerage (Englehardt & Narayanan; ICCL on real-time bidding; FTC 2014; California's data broker registry), enforcement (DLA Piper and CMS GDPR fine totals; California's Sephora/GPC settlement) and the AI-chatbot base on which agents are built (Pew 2025; NBER/OpenAI 2025). Method: every quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and re-checked with --check in a final audit (95 unique source-quote pairs; all FOUND except the three Obar & Oeldorf-Hirsch quotes, which come from a JSON API and were verified against the decoded abstract instead — see their notes). quant.geography: EU: privacy policies of the 500 most popular websites in each of the 28 member states (6,579 sites in the study; 2016 lengths from Internet Archive copies)
quant.notes: Up from a mean of 2,145 words in March 2016 and 3,044 words in March 2018. Policies grew by about two-thirds (+68%) in just over two years. The 2016 figure is based on Internet Archive copies (on average 2,187 policies a month could be retrieved), so the three means are not necessarily over the same set of sites. The authors did not compare lengths across countries because of language differences. (Amos et al. 2021 cite the 2016 and 2018 figures as medians; Degeling et al. describe them as means.)

The notes say the growth happened 'most of it around the GDPR'. That is wrong if it means the deadline. Of the 1,458 words added (2,145 to 3,603, +68%, so 'about two-thirds' is right), 899 (62%) were added between March 2016 and March 2018. The paper's 'another 18 percentage points' is measured against the March 2018 length (3,603/3,044 = +18%), not the 2016 base (which would be +26 points).

The notes leave out a population caveat. The March 2016 (and 2017) lengths come from Internet Archive copies. The paper says 'On average, we were able to access previous versions for 2,187 policies for each month'. So the 2016 mean is not over all 6,579 sites, and the three means are not necessarily over the same set of policies. issues: Both quotes are verbatim in the live ICCL PDF. 747, Colorado 987, District of Columbia 486 ('D.C. day time commuter adjusted population used') and the lowest state, Mississippi 493, all match the per-person chart on p. 3.

The 747 is not total U.S. broadcasts divided by population. It equals the simple unweighted mean of ICCL's 51 state and D.C. figures (746.7). ICCL's own total of 294 billion a day divided by the 2021 U.S. population (about 332 million) gives about 886, or about 984 if divided by 90% of the population. The notes should say what the 747 is.

The notes misdescribe the stated method. They say per-person figures 'divide by population assuming 90% of people are online'. The published state and country figures instead match 0.9 x daily broadcasts / total population, within 1%, for every state or country where the report gives a daily total: California 35bn gives 803 (published 804), Texas 24.5bn gives 747 (748), Florida 21bn gives 868 (870), Germany 30.8bn gives 333 (334), France 25.4bn gives 339 (340), using 2021 census and Eurostat populations. Dividing by 90% of the population would give figures about 23% higher. The UK (31.9bn a day, published 462) fits neither method.
'State averages range from 987 (Colorado) to 486 (District of Columbia...)': D.C. is not a state. Reworded to 'state and D.C. figures'.

The report does not reconcile internally. ICCL says 'People in the U.S. have their online activity and real-world location exposed 57% more often than people in Europe', but 747 vs 376 is 99% more. The Europe 376 also seems to use a different method (see the Europe verdict), so the U.S. and Europe headline averages should not be compared directly.
The notes leave out ICCL's own caveat. The report calls its figures 'a low estimate' because the industry data exclude Facebook and Amazon RTB broadcasts.

No independent source reproduces the figure, because the underlying industry data are confidential. The session's web-search budget was exhausted, so press coverage could not be looked for. The record is kept as a clearly labelled advocacy estimate. Year 2022 (publication 16 May 2022, per the page's article:published_time) is right.

myths.correction: Cookie consent predates the GDPR: a 2009 amendment (Directive 2009/136/EC) to the EU's ePrivacy Directive already made storing information on a user's device conditional on consent (strictly necessary cookies excepted), and in January 2018, months before the GDPR applied on 25 May 2018, 46.1% of the sites on the 500-most-popular lists of the 28 EU member states already showed a cookie consent notice. Many still fell short of the law's own standard for consent: a September 2019 scrape of 680 top UK sites using the five most popular consent platforms found only 11.8% met minimal requirements of EU law.

myths.claim: Clicking 'accept' on a consent pop-up is a free, informed choice.
myths.correction: When Nouwens and colleagues scraped the top 10,000 UK websites in September 2019 for the five most popular consent platforms, only 11.8% of the 680 sites using them met three minimal requirements of EU law (explicit consent, rejecting as easy as accepting, no pre-ticked boxes), and half had no 'reject all' button. myths.claim: If you clear your cookies, websites can no longer track you.
myths.correction: Tracking also works without stored identifiers. Englehardt and Narayanan's January 2016 crawl of the top million sites found canvas fingerprinting, which identifies a device from the tiny differences in how it draws the same image, on 14,371 sites, 98.2% of it from third-party scripts. The authors noted that its use had shifted from behavioural tracking toward fraud detection, but such fingerprints need no cookie. They warned that another device readout they found in fingerprinting scripts 'may remain constant when a user clears cookies, switches to private browsing mode, or opens a new browser'.

issues: The figures are right. The crawl is the January 2016 measurement of the Alexa top 1 million: canvas fingerprinting on 14,371 sites (1.6% of the 917,261 sites successfully measured), 98.2% from third-party scripts.

The correction leaves out the paper's own caveat, which weakens how it uses the number as evidence of tracking. On the same page the authors write that 'the most prominent trackers have by-and-large stopped using it' and that 'the use has shifted from behavioral tracking to fraud detection'. Presenting the 14,371 sites as tracking without this is misleading. The fix adds the caveat.

The correction never shows that fingerprinting survives cookie clearing, which is the myth's actual point. The paper says so directly for a device readout (the Battery Status API): 'the readout may remain constant when a user clears cookies'. That quote is added.

'draws hidden graphics' is not what the paper says. It describes devices drawing the same image differently ('Differences in font rendering, smoothing, anti-aliasing ... cause devices to draw the image differently'). The wording is adjusted.

myths.claim: The GDPR is toothless: regulators never fine anyone.
myths.correction: Fines are real and large: about EUR 7.1 billion from 25 May 2018 to 10 January 2026 by DLA Piper's count, including a single EUR 1.2 billion fine on Meta in 2023. But they are concentrated on a few big-tech firms and a few regulators. Ireland alone accounts for about EUR 4.04 billion, and every one of the ten largest fines in CMS's tracker, nine of them Irish, fell on Meta (including WhatsApp), TikTok, LinkedIn or Uber. Totals also differ by method: CMS counts about EUR 6.11 billion of publicly known fines to 1 March 2026. The fair criticism is uneven, slow enforcement, not absence of enforcement: in 2021 the Irish Council for Civil Liberties found 98% of major GDPR cases referred to Ireland still unresolved.
